## Statement of Need

In the Eastside neighborhood (zip 12345), children are falling behind in reading at twice the rate of their peers statewide, and the local supports families have historically relied on are shrinking. According to the State Department of Education (2024), 28% of Eastside third graders read below grade level, compared with 14% statewide. Third-grade reading proficiency is one of the most reliable predictors of long-term academic success: students who are not reading on grade level by the end of third grade are four times more likely to leave school without a diploma. In Eastside, that risk is concentrated among children who already face significant economic disadvantage.

The neighborhood's child poverty rate is 40%, more than twice the countywide rate of 18% (American Community Survey, 2023). Poverty compounds the reading gap in well-documented ways: fewer books in the home, less access to paid enrichment, higher rates of housing instability, and caregivers working multiple jobs with limited time for nightly reading routines. For Eastside families, these pressures are daily realities rather than abstract risk factors, and they translate directly into the proficiency gap captured in state testing data.

This gap has widened since the pandemic, and the community infrastructure that once helped buffer it is weakening. The local branch of the public library reports a 30% drop in summer reading program attendance since 2019, removing one of the few free, consistent literacy touchpoints available to Eastside children during the months when learning loss accelerates most sharply. At the same time, there are few afterschool literacy options within a two-mile radius of the neighborhood's elementary schools, leaving families with limited practical alternatives, particularly those without reliable transportation.

Demand for the supports that do exist far outstrips supply. [Organization] currently maintains a waitlist of 120 children for our tutoring program, with an average wait of six months (organizational records, 2024). Six months is not a neutral delay: it can span an entire academic semester, during which a struggling reader falls further behind peers and loses confidence in the classroom. Every month a child waits is a month in which the intervention becomes harder and the gap more entrenched.

Residents themselves have identified this as their most urgent concern. In a 2024 community survey of Eastside parents and caregivers (n=86), respondents named "help with my child's reading" as the top priority for new neighborhood services, ahead of other commonly cited needs. Parents described wanting consistent, free, nearby tutoring and summer programs, and expressed frustration at waitlists and the disappearance of library offerings. Their voices align with the quantitative picture: a community that recognizes its children are at risk and is actively asking for help.

Why now? Three forces are converging. First, the proficiency gap captured in the most recent state data is the widest Eastside has seen in a decade, meaning more children are entering fourth grade without the foundational skills they need. Second, the free community programs that previously absorbed some of this demand, including the library's summer offerings, are contracting rather than expanding. Third, our own waitlist has grown to a point where families who seek help today will not receive it until the following school year, by which time the critical third-grade window will have closed for many of them.

Eastside's children are facing a measurable, documented, and worsening literacy crisis, in a neighborhood with concentrated poverty, shrinking public supports, and overwhelmed nonprofit capacity. Expanding tutoring now is the most direct way to close the gap before it becomes permanent.

---

We will serve 180 children annually, primarily residents of zip 12345 in kindergarten through third grade who are reading below grade level or at risk of falling behind. Eligibility is based on three criteria: current enrollment in grades K–3, residence in the Eastside neighborhood (zip 12345), and either a demonstrated reading skill gap or qualification for free or reduced-price school meals as an indicator of economic need. Verification will occur at intake through a short enrollment packet: proof of residence (utility bill, lease, or school enrollment record), a school-issued reading level or teacher referral form, and a signed caregiver application. For children referred directly by partner schools, teacher documentation will serve as the primary verification.

Demographically, participants will reflect the Eastside neighborhood: children ages 5 to 9, concentrated in households with incomes below the federal poverty line, and attending the two elementary schools that serve zip 12345. Across a three-year grant period, we expect to serve approximately 540 unduplicated children, with some returning for multiple years of support.

This population carries the highest literacy risk in the county. They also face the thinnest safety net: few afterschool literacy options exist within a two-mile radius, and the local library's summer program, once a key resource, has lost 30% of its attendance since 2019. Meanwhile, 120 children are already waiting an average of six months for tutoring through our organization (org records, 2024). These children are not underserved by accident; they live in a neighborhood where need is concentrated and supply has contracted at the same time.

## Program Design & Activities

### Logic of Change

Eastside children fall behind in reading because they lack three things at once: consistent, individualized instruction outside the school day; literacy-rich routines and materials at home; and continuous learning opportunities during the summer months when gaps widen fastest. Our program addresses all three simultaneously. By pairing children with trained tutors for sustained one-on-one instruction, equipping caregivers to reinforce reading at home, and providing an intensive summer booster to prevent learning loss, we aim to move participants from below grade level to on grade level in reading by the end of third grade. Each component is designed to reinforce the others, so that gains made during tutoring are sustained at home and protected across the summer.

### Participant Pathway

Children enter through school referrals, caregiver self-referrals, or our waitlist. **Intake** (weeks 1–2 of each cycle) includes a reading assessment using an established tool (DIBELS or equivalent), goal-setting with the caregiver, and tutor matching. **Services** (weeks 3–14) consist of twice-weekly tutoring, monthly family literacy nights, and ongoing progress monitoring every six weeks. **Exit and follow-up** occur in weeks 15–16, with a repeat assessment, a caregiver debrief, a summer plan, and enrollment into the summer booster where appropriate. Children who have not yet reached grade level re-enter the next tutoring cycle; those who have reached grade level receive quarterly check-ins for one year to monitor retention.

### Core Activity 1: One-on-One Tutoring

Addresses the 28% below-grade-level rate and the 120-child waitlist. Cohorts of 30 children per 14-week cycle, with three cycles per year, will serve 90 unduplicated children annually in this component. Each child receives two 45-minute sessions per week with a trained tutor, totaling 21 hours of individualized instruction per cycle. Sessions take place at two partner school sites and at our neighborhood center, all within zip 12345 to eliminate transportation barriers. Tutors use a structured literacy approach aligned with the science of reading, emphasizing phonemic awareness, decoding, fluency, and comprehension. One-on-one tutoring delivered with this frequency and dosage is among the most evidence-supported interventions for early literacy, consistently producing meaningful gains for struggling readers in the primary grades. **Rubric link (Program Design, 30%):** clear logic, documented dosage, evidence-based approach, and direct line from the stated need (reading gap, waitlist) to activity.

### Core Activity 2: Family Literacy Nights

Addresses the home-environment dimension of the reading gap in a high-poverty neighborhood and responds to the community survey finding that caregivers want practical tools to help their children read. We will host one family literacy night per month during the school year (9 per year), serving an estimated 60 families and 120 children across the year, with duplication across months expected. Each two-hour evening at a partner school includes a shared meal, a modeled read-aloud, a hands-on activity caregivers can replicate at home, and a free book for every child to build home libraries. Engaging caregivers as literacy partners is a well-established best practice for sustaining classroom and tutoring gains, particularly for children from low-income households where access to books and reading time can be limited. **Rubric link (Program Design, 30%):** activity tied explicitly to community voice data and poverty indicator, with clear dosage, location, and reach.

### Core Activity 3: Eight-Week Summer Reading Booster

Addresses summer learning loss, intensified by the 30% decline in library summer program attendance since 2019. Two cohorts of 45 children (90 total annually) will attend a half-day program four days per week for eight weeks at a partner school site, totaling approximately 128 hours of summer instruction per child. Programming combines small-group guided reading, independent reading time, read-alouds, and enrichment activities co-designed with the local library, which will provide books, librarian visits, and library card sign-ups. Sustained, multi-week summer literacy programming is a recognized best practice for preventing the summer slide that disproportionately affects children in low-income neighborhoods. **Rubric link (Program Design, 30%):** targets a specific, documented local gap (library decline) and a known risk window.

### Reach Summary

Total unduplicated children served annually: 180 (90 tutoring + 90 summer booster, with family literacy nights reinforcing both groups).

### Partnerships

Two Eastside elementary schools will provide referrals, assessment data sharing (with caregiver consent), and site space. The local public library will co-design summer programming, provide books and librarian hours, and host culminating events. A local teacher-preparation program will supply tutor candidates for training and supervision. MOUs are in place or in progress with each partner.

### Quarterly Timeline (Year 1)

**Q1:** Hire and train staff and tutors; finalize partnerships; launch Cycle 1 tutoring (30 children) and first family literacy nights.
**Q2:** Complete Cycle 1, launch Cycle 2 tutoring (30 children), continue monthly literacy nights.
**Q3:** Complete Cycle 2, run 8-week summer booster (90 children across two cohorts), mid-year evaluation.
**Q4:** Launch Cycle 3 tutoring (30 children), resume literacy nights, annual evaluation and reporting.

## Outcomes & Objectives (~400 words)

This program is designed to produce measurable change at three levels: participant reading skill, access to services, and sustained community literacy engagement. Each objective below is tied to a local baseline drawn from the Statement of Need, with specific targets, timeframes, measurement tools, and a clear distinction between outputs (what we deliver) and outcomes (what changes for participants).

### Objective 1 (Outcome): Improve Reading Proficiency

By the end of each program year, at least 65% of participating children in grades K–3 will advance at least one reading level or move from below grade level to on grade level, measured against their intake assessment. *Baseline:* 28% of Eastside third graders currently read below grade level, compared with 14% statewide (State Department of Education, 2024); participants will enter with individual baselines established at intake. *Measurement:* DIBELS (or equivalent structured literacy assessment) administered at intake, mid-cycle (week 8), and exit (week 14), plus a retention check six months post-exit for a sample of participants. *Rubric link:* measurable outcome with documented baseline and validated measurement method.

### Objective 2 (Output and Access): Reduce Waitlist and Expand Reach

Within the first program year, we will serve 120 unduplicated children and reduce the current tutoring waitlist of 120 children by at least 50%, cutting average wait time from 6 months to no more than 3 months. *Baseline:* 120 children on the waitlist with a 6-month average wait (organizational records, 2024). *Measurement:* enrollment records, intake date logs, and monthly waitlist reports generated by the Family & Community Liaison. *Rubric link:* access outcome tied directly to a documented local baseline; output (120 served) is distinguished from outcome (reduced wait time).

### Objective 3 (Outcome): Strengthen Family and Community Literacy Engagement

By the end of Year 1, at least 75% of participating caregivers will report increased confidence supporting their child's reading at home, and summer booster enrollment will restore community summer literacy participation to within 10% of the 2019 library baseline. *Baseline:* library summer program attendance down 30% since 2019; caregiver confidence to be measured at intake. *Measurement:* pre/post caregiver surveys at intake and program exit, family literacy night attendance logs, and shared summer enrollment data with the library partner. *Rubric link:* outcome (confidence, participation levels) tied to community voice data and documented local trend.

### Phrasing Hooks for the Application

"By [date], 65% of participants will advance at least one reading level, up from a baseline of individually assessed below-grade-level entry (measured by DIBELS at intake, mid-cycle, and exit)."

"We will reduce the Eastside tutoring waitlist by 50% in Year 1, cutting average wait time from 6 months to 3 months, measured through enrollment and intake records."

"At least 75% of caregivers will report increased confidence supporting reading at home, measured by pre/post surveys, while summer literacy participation is restored to near pre-2019 levels in partnership with the public library."
